title: The Future Of AI Compute Won’t Run On Just One Kind Of Chip
gist: An expert panel argues AI data centers are shifting from GPU-only clusters to heterogeneous clusters of CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, custom ASICs and optics, driven by inference disaggregation, token-cost economics, and power limits. Software orchestration across multi-vendor hardware and Nvidia's software moat emerge as the central competitive battlegrounds.

insights.claim: AI inference is being disaggregated into separate clusters for prefill, decode, and agent execution, each with a different mix of hardware and software and stitched together mostly over Ethernet.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Disaggregation opens the accelerator stack to non-GPU silicon at specific pipeline stages, expanding the addressable market beyond Nvidia GPUs.
insights.quote: you have a cluster with a specific set of hardware and software to do the pre-filled stage. Then, you have a cluster to do the decode stage, and then you have another fully compute cluster to do the execution by the agents.

insights.claim: Nvidia announced that its Groq 3 LPU (language processing unit) will be used in the prefill cluster, indicating more than a GPU is required for some inference tasks.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Signals GPU vendors themselves adopting specialized non-GPU silicon for compute-intensive prefill, validating heterogeneous inference.
insights.quote: Recently, Nvidia announced that its Groq 3 LPU (language processing unit) will be used in the prefill cluster, showing more than a GPU is required to do some of these tasks.

insights.claim: The prefill stage of inference is extremely compute-intensive while decode generates the response and agents perform the tool-calling execution such as booking an Uber or a hotel.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Distinct workload characteristics per stage justify matching different silicon to each, reshaping accelerator demand.

insights.claim: The industry is recognizing that not every AI problem should be solved with a GPU, driving a shift to heterogeneous clusters where diverse hardware from different companies must be coordinated by software.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Multi-vendor heterogeneous hardware is the structural bet against single-vendor GPU dominance.
insights.quote: every AI problem was solved with a GPU, and the industry is recognizing that every nail doesn’t have one hammer.

insights.claim: DigitalOcean announced deployment of a five-layer architecture for inference tuned to use heterogeneous clusters underneath, referencing both AMD and Nvidia hardware.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Neoclouds building explicitly multi-vendor inference stacks show demand pull for AMD and others alongside Nvidia.

insights.claim: Reasoning-heavy and agentic inference does not make accelerators less important but segments the pipeline, letting control-heavy, stateful, branchy steps and massively parallel tensor math run on different engines within one coherent hybrid system.
insights.speaker: Moshiko Emmer
insights.so_what: Hybrid architectures displace forcing one compute type to do everything inefficiently, favoring composable multi-engine SoCs.
insights.quote: It’s that the pipeline becomes more segmented. Some steps are control-heavy, stateful, and branchy. Others are still massively parallel tensor math.

insights.claim: Reasoning can run on accelerators that need not be GPUs—a custom ASIC can do the matrix-multiplication-heavy reasoning function—while orchestration and tool-calling by agents run on CPUs under tight software control.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Custom ASICs are positioned as direct substitutes for GPUs in the reasoning step, a competitive opening for custom silicon.
insights.quote: I’ll use the word accelerators instead of GPUs, because it doesn’t have to be a GPU. It can be a custom ASIC that does the reasoning function.

insights.claim: As models have grown, memory has become a critical bottleneck, making the cost and utilization of HBM a decisive factor for GPUs, with the dynamic context portion of models driving how many requests can be processed per second.
insights.speaker: Sharad Chole
insights.so_what: HBM cost and utilization gate data-center throughput economics, reinforcing memory suppliers' pricing power.
insights.quote: the memory became one of the critical bottlenecks that needed to be utilized with the computations. That’s where the cost of HBM, and how the HBM is utilized, become very important factors for GPUs.

insights.claim: Different parallelization paradigms—tensor, data, context, and pipeline parallel—each impose a different network topology requirement, which is why NVLink is important for scaling out tensor-parallel topologies.
insights.speaker: Sharad Chole
insights.so_what: Interconnect choice is dictated by parallelization strategy, entrenching NVLink where tensor-parallel scaling dominates.
insights.quote: That’s why NVLink is one of the important parts if you have to scale out to tensor parallel topologies.

insights.claim: Google TPUs use optical interconnect instead of copper, and more optical interconnects are expected over the next few years to meet the escalating demand for speed.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: A copper-to-optics transition in the datacenter interconnect is a multi-year tailwind for co-packaged-optics and photonics suppliers.
insights.quote: there are Google TPUs, and they have decided to use optics for connection — optical interconnect, which is light, not copper.

insights.claim: Co-packaged optics is an emerging research area aimed at bringing photonic connections closer to and within the chip, motivated by photons' speed advantage and near-zero energy dissipation versus electrical links.
insights.speaker: Sumit Vishwakarma
insights.so_what: Co-packaged optics targets both bandwidth and the cooling-cost problem, a key emerging design and supply category.
insights.quote: It’s electrons versus photons, and photons are faster. There’s no resistance and minimal or no energy dissipation.

insights.claim: Interconnects separate into three architectural layers—chiplet/package, node-level coherent host-to-accelerator attachment, and cluster fabric—and the goal is well-matched fabrics with minimal impedance mismatch rather than one universal fabric.
insights.speaker: Moshiko Emmer
insights.so_what: Every boundary conversion costs latency and energy, so standardization at each layer determines system efficiency and vendor interoperability.
insights.quote: You do not need one universal fabric. You need well-matched fabrics with minimal impedance mismatch.

insights.claim: Emerging die-to-die standards such as UCIe are making chip-to-chip links more interoperable and predictable across vendors, which is critical for building larger coherent nodes out of multiple chiplets.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Interoperable die-to-die standards enable multi-vendor chiplet nodes, underpinning the heterogeneous-hardware thesis.
insights.quote: Industry standards such as UCIe are emerging to make those die‑to‑die links more interoperable and predictable across vendors.

insights.claim: In cluster-to-cluster interconnect, Ethernet remains the broad standard while HPE's Slingshot and InfiniBand compete, with Slingshot the highest-performing but locked to HPE Cray systems.
insights.speaker: Cameron Brunner
insights.so_what: Proprietary fabrics win on performance but Ethernet's breadth keeps catching up, framing the interconnect ecosystem choice for buyers.
insights.quote: There’s been investment over the years where a team will come in and make a new dedicated protocol to do something that Ethernet can’t do, but history has shown that just motivates Ethernet to improve.

insights.claim: Heterogeneous compute packages combining GPU, accelerator, NPU, CPU and HBM face multi-physics risks such as heat, warpage and electromigration that can collapse multi-die HBM stacks and degrade whole-cluster performance.
insights.speaker: Sumit Vishwakarma
insights.so_what: Package-level thermal and reliability effects propagate to cluster performance, raising the design and verification stakes for advanced packaging.
insights.quote: If it were multi-die HBM, it might collapse because of heat or warpage. The whole node will be impacted. The AI cluster will get impacted.

insights.claim: Nvidia's key moat is no longer its hardware but the software ecosystem it has built over 20-plus years, making it a tuned complete hardware-software solution that scales.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: The competitive barrier to displacing Nvidia is software, not silicon, so challengers must solve heterogeneous orchestration to win.
insights.quote: One of the moats that Nvidia has is not their hardware anymore. It’s their software ecosystem that they have built over the last 20-plus years.

insights.claim: Startups such as Gimlet Labs and Together AI are positioning as the software layer that runs heterogeneous hardware and disaggregated inference, optimizing prefill, decode and compute clusters across multiple vendors.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: A new software-orchestration layer is where value accrues if the heterogeneous-hardware transition succeeds—worth tracking as investable challengers to CUDA lock-in.
insights.quote: Their pitch is that they provide the software layer to run on top of a heterogeneous hardware environment, even on disaggregated inference
insights.locator: Bhattacharjee, Gimlet Labs and Together AI

insights.claim: Neoclouds including DigitalOcean, CoreWeave, Lambda AI and Verda all face the same challenge of adding hardware diversity and cutting token costs without a single vendor holding their hand, while everyone still waits in line for Nvidia systems.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Nvidia supply scarcity plus token-cost pressure is the demand driver pushing neoclouds toward heterogeneous alternatives.
insights.quote: everybody is waiting in line for Nvidia systems because that’s the only system that is proven to be working at scale right now.

insights.claim: Containers, not virtual machines, have become the standard AI deployment method, wrapping runtime, orchestration, scheduling, queuing, API endpoints and serving platforms—with agentic coding making it easier to build specialized stacks.
insights.speaker: Sharad Chole
insights.so_what: Containerized, specialized software stacks are the deployment substrate that heterogeneous-hardware orchestration must plug into.
insights.quote: in the AI world, containers have caught up pretty much everywhere. That’s the standard way of bringing things up

insights.claim: At a high level power is the number-one problem for cluster design because without power nothing works, with token efficiency—delivered through heterogeneity—the second challenge.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee
insights.so_what: Power and token cost are the two constraints ranking above raw compute, framing where AI-infrastructure capex and innovation flow.
insights.quote: At a high level, power is definitely the number one problem. Without power, nothing will work. The second challenge is token efficiency
